Line 3: the sentence after 'Dignum et justum est' ('quem justa et digna oratione...') is garbled; translated for the evident sense. Line 6: deriving 'Deus' from 'diligendo' is the text's own etymology. Line 11: 'omnes praedicatores' ('all the preachers') may be a corruption of 'praedicti ordines' ('the aforesaid orders'), which would fit the context better. Line 12: the text says 'twenty-four living creatures'; Revelation 4 has four living creatures and twenty-four elders. Line 13: 'salum fac' read as 'salvum fac'; 'monte Vii veri' read as 'monte Oliveti'; 'flectemur' read as 'flectetur'.

§23 is numbered '25' in the scan; read 23. §16: 'Bona sunt' read as 'Dona sunt' (gifts), matching the lemma. 'in nullo capite' taken as 'in a certain chapter' (likely 'in illo capite'); as printed it would mean 'in no chapter'. §22: 'ut illa oblatione ... ut ... faciat' is syntactically garbled; rendered by joining to the following lemma. §19 'hi primis' read 'in primis'.

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'misericordix' as misericordiae, 'meriti' for 'merisi', 'salus æterna' for 'salus alterni', 'idem' as 'id est', 'facta sum' as 'facta sunt', 'opeibus ... qma perceptionem lidei' as 'operibus ... quod per perceptionem fidei', 'omnes vicus' as 'omnes victus'. In 33 'credere ... in Panem cœlestem' is taken as 'Patrem cœlestem'. In 35 'Panis apud Græcos' refers to Greek *pan* ('all'). The Matthew 13:41 citation is loose ('auferuntur' for 'colligent'). Bracketed editorial conjectures ('Forte ...') followed where they clarify; '(corpus)' in 30 is an editorial supplement.
In 41 the garbled 'III v muntiat ... nullus :mea exire ... quam nuntiatum' is read as 'Ille nuntiat ... nullus ante exire ... antequam nuntiatum'. In 38 'nagella' is read as 'flagella'.

nodes.text: APPENDIX VIII.
EXPLANATION OF THE MASS.

1. *The Lord be with you* (*Vita Isidoriana*, ch. 84). He greets the people and prays that the Lord may be with them. *And with your spirit*: the people's response, and a prayer that, just as the priest prayed that the Lord might be with the people, so the people too pray that the Lord may be with the priest's spirit. When the priest says *Let us pray*, he asks everyone to pray that his prayer may be heard by the Lord. And when he says *Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son*, the priest prays to the Lord the Father that the prayer may be accomplished through his Son, who is our Lord equally, as the Father is. When he says *Who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit*, he wants the people to believe and understand that the Son lives and reigns with the Father without beginning and without end, and is God, as the Father is God; and that there is one power of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, and one substance, and in all things a unity of deity.

2. *For ever and ever.* Let it be believed that the same Son, with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, just as he existed and lived in deity before all ages, so also in the present age, and in the age to come, where the just will remain with the holy angels and the unjust will be tormented with the devil, lives equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and is confined by no end. *Amen* is the people's confirmation of the prayer, and in our language it can be understood as though all were saying: 'May it be so, as the priest has prayed'; but its proper meaning is: 'Truly', or 'Faithfully'.

3. *Lift up your hearts.* The priest admonishes the people to lift their hearts upward, that is, above themselves, to the almighty Lord, and to pray faithfully that help may come to them from above from the heavenly Lord, by whom all things were created. *We have [them] to the Lord*: the people's response, that just as the priest commanded them to hold their hearts upward, so they profess that they keep [them there]. *Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.* The priest gives thanks to God in accordance with the people's profession, because they have confessed that they are intent on the Lord. *It is fitting and right.* The people together with the priest give thanks to God, [saying] that it is with a right and fitting prayer that we render thanks to God, because we have received all good things from him, in the name of the Lord. Amen.

4. *It is truly fitting and right, just and salutary.* The priest confirms the people's profession and says that it is truly fitting and right to render thanks to God for all things; and that it is just, that is, right or equitable; and salutary, that is, full of salvation, that we should render thanks to him who has given us eternal salvation. *That we should always and everywhere give thanks to you.* After the people's profession the priest, turned towards the Lord, speaks as if to one present, because we are always in the presence of the Lord, since he sees our thoughts; and the priest says that he gives thanks both on his own behalf and on the people's. *Lord*, because he is ruler of all, and all things are under his rule. *Holy*, because he is holy, and [the one] through whom all things are holy, because you created all things holy and good. *Father*: in Greek we say *pater*, in Latin *genitor* ['begetter'], because he begot the Son without any defilement or corruption.

5. In Latin *pater* is said to come from *patrare*, that is, from *perpetrare*, which means 'to accomplish', or from 'helping', because he made all things that have been made. And he helps all things that are helped, and willed that we should become his adopted sons through sanctification, by which he sanctified us. *Almighty*: because he can do all things, he is therefore called almighty, and no word is impossible with God. *Eternal God*: here [one must distinguish] between eternal, perpetual and temporal. Eternal is what has no beginning and will have no end, but always was, and is, and will be. Perpetual is what began to exist and will have no end. Temporal is what had a beginning and will have an end.

6. And therefore it is said here *Eternal God*, because he neither began to exist nor ceases to exist, but always is. *Deus* ['God'] is said to come from *diligere* ['to love'], because he loves, governs and created all things. And otherwise *Deus* is named from divinity, because he is divine, and knows all things, and divides all things as he wills.

7. *Through Christ our Lord.* *Christus* is Greek; in Latin it is said *unctus* ['anointed']. This Christ was begotten of the Father ineffably before all beginnings; when it pleased him, the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin Mary and anointed her womb with a divine anointing, and he was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.

8. For in the Old Testament too priests and kings were anointed, and were therefore called *christi* ['anointed ones'], because they were anointed with a temporal anointing. This Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, is Christ eternally, and is called eternal with the Father; and through him, through whom we give thanks to the Father, we have been redeemed; and he is our Lord God, because he rules over us. *Through whom the angels praise your majesty.* Through Christ himself, through whom we give thanks to the Father, the angels praise the Father's majesty, because he is equal to the Father in divinity. *Majestas* ['majesty'], because the power of God is greater (*major*) than that of men. The angels praise God's majesty through Christ, because Christ together with the Father created the angels.

9. For *angelus* is Greek; in Latin it is rendered *nuntius* ['messenger']. 'Angel' is the name of an office, not of a nature, because it announces; but by nature they are spirits. *The dominations adore.* The dominations praise and adore the majesty of God the Father through the Son. The dominations are an order of angels. There were ten orders of angels. The tenth order fell and through pride was turned into the devil. But nine remained in their holiness. These are their names: angels, archangels, virtues, principalities, powers, thrones, dominations, cherubim, seraphim. The names of these last two are not Latin. Cherubim is rendered 'fullness of knowledge'. Seraphim is said to mean 'burning'. The other names of the aforesaid orders are Latin, except those of the angels and archangels. Angels are called 'messengers', archangels 'exalted messengers'.

10. But Gregory, the Roman pope, in his homily on the Gospel reading *The publicans and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him*, explained these orders most fully. Let us, however, return to our subject. *The powers tremble.* This is said of the aforesaid orders: he does not say it because the aforesaid orders are bodily, but he speaks after our manner, because we are accustomed to tremble and fear before our lords. But he says 'tremble' so that we may understand that all things in heaven, on earth and in the underworld tremble and fear before the sight of the divine Majesty.

11. *The heavens and the virtues of the heavens.* The heavens themselves obey the divine sight, because they have no power to show themselves clear or cloudy. The virtues of the heavens are the aforesaid orders of angels, as Gregory testifies in his homily on the Gospel reading *There will be signs in the sun, moon and stars*. *And the blessed seraphim.* Of the seraphim mention has been made above. *Celebrate together in shared exultation.* All the preachers celebrate together the majesty of God the Father through Christ, equally, with united exultation. *With whom.* This is our supplication: that the heavenly Father himself, through Christ his Son, through whom we give him thanks for all things, may deign to admit our voices and join them to the voices of the aforesaid orders of angels.

12. *Saying in humble confession.* That is, in lowly confession. What humbler confession is there than to commend ourselves to the eternal Father through the eternal Son, and to presume nothing from our own conscience or goodness, and, in accordance with the angelic voices, always to believe and proclaim him holy in his essence? *Holy, Holy, Holy.* John the Evangelist wrote in the book of the Apocalypse that he saw before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four living creatures standing and saying unceasingly: *Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth*, etc. For *Holy* is said three times to signify that the Father is holy, the Son is holy, the Spirit of the Father and the Son is holy. But although 'holy' is said three times, yet we do not say in the plural 'holy ones', but in the singular 'holy', so that one holiness and one eternity may be understood in these three persons.

13. *Lord God Sabaoth.* Sabaoth is commonly rendered by many as 'almighty', but by many as 'of hosts', meaning that he himself is Lord God and he himself orders all the hosts of angels and of men. *Heaven and earth are full of your glory.* The same: that by his glory heaven and earth are governed, and that those who are in heaven and those who are on earth glorify and honour his name. *Hosanna in the highest.* How [is it that] it is now said, corruptly, *Osanna*? Formerly it was said *Osiana*. *Osi* is an interjection of one praising, or of one magnifying. *Anna* [means] 'save'. But it is said corruptly *Osanna*, and can be understood as 'save' or 'make safe'. *In the highest*, that is, in the heights. *Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.* When Christ came to Jerusalem and came down from the Mount of Olives, then the children of Israel cried out, saying: *Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord*; but what did that coming of Christ to Jerusalem signify, if not the future resurrection, when he will come to judge the living and the dead, and will appear to us in the same flesh in which he suffered for us? And then at the name of Jesus every knee shall bend, of things in heaven, on earth and in the underworld, etc., as the Apostle said.

14. *Therefore you, most merciful Father.* *Therefore you*: that is, you surely, most merciful Father. He is called *clemens* [merciful] as if *clara mens* [clear mind], or abounding; and *clementissime*, as if with most clear mind, or most abundantly, because he himself is most clear in mind, and a most merciful Father. We do not call him merciful and compassionate on the ground that he is composed of bodily members, or heart, or mind, as a man is; but we cry out that he is merciful and compassionate so that we may feel that mercy and compassion upon us from him, and may understand whence we are to be saved.

15. *Through Jesus Christ.* *Jesus* is Greek; in Latin he is called Saviour, or Bringer of salvation. Saviour, because he saves his people from their sins. He saves from sins because he has the power of forgiving sins, as he himself said: *But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins* (Matt. 9:6). He is called Bringer of salvation because he gave us salvation, so that, if we keep his commandments, we may be able to receive eternal life. *Your Son*: namely your only-begotten Son, because he is the only-begotten from the substance of the Father, while we are adoptive sons through him who is the only-begotten, proceeding from the Father, coeternal with the Father; and therefore through him we entreat the Father, saying humbly:

16. *As suppliants we ask and beseech you.* Suppliants, that is, humble. *That you may hold acceptable and bless.* *Uti*, that is, that you may accept and bless. *These gifts, these offerings, these holy unblemished sacrifices.* Gifts are what are given willingly. Offerings are what are offered in return for some reward and payment, as we offer to God that our sins may be forgiven. Sacrifices are what are already consecrated with prayers. *Illibata* is the same as immaculate, and free from all the stain of malice. Gifts and sacrifices are unblemished when they are offered without the stains of offences, and acquired by just labour. Not, as many err who say that *illibata* means not dedicated. Read the *Conferences* of the Fathers, and in the second conference of Theonas, in a certain chapter, you will find what things are unblemished.

17. *First, which we offer to you.* That is, *which we offer to you*; they indicate for whom they are offered: first they ought to be offered for your holy catholic Church. *Ecclesia* is Greek; in Latin it is called congregation. *Catholic* means universal, because all who believe in the Lord ought to be in one congregation. *Which may you deign to give peace, guard, unite and govern throughout the whole world.* May you deign to guard [it], given peace and united throughout the whole world. *Together with your servant N.* That is, together with him who holds the see of the apostle Peter, because the Church in which Peter, prince of the apostles, sat is the head of all catholic Churches. [This is] because Christ says to Peter: *You are Peter, and on this rock*, and the rest (Matt. 16:18). And on account of this saying we ought all to pray for him who is in that same Church.

18. *And our bishop N.*, that is, for the bishop; he is our shepherd and preacher. *Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids, and all those standing around.* The priest has already prayed for the apostolic [pontiff] and for his bishop. If a bishop celebrates Mass, he ought not to say 'for our bishop', because he himself is the bishop. If a priest celebrates Mass, he ought to say 'for our bishop'. Prayer has now been made for the elders; next prayer must be made for the people. When the priest says *Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids*, he beseeches the Lord the Father to deign to remember all, whether men or women, who come to the office of the Mass. And when he says *those standing around*, the men and women themselves are meant, whoever are standing by.

19. Now the priest has prayed for all who came to hear Mass; then at last he prays for those who bring their offerings. *Who offer you this sacrifice of praise.* It is called [a sacrifice] of praise because they offer first for the praise of God, and afterwards for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and safety; *and render their vows to you*, the eternal God, living and true. They offer for this reason, that to the living and true God the faith of all who stand around, those offering and those not offering, is known, and their devotion is recognised. All render their vows. They are called *vota* [vows] because they are promised *volenter* [willingly], since we ought to vow willingly and gladly. *In communion, and venerating the memory, first of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.*

20. To be in communion, that is, to share in the memory; to venerate, that is, to hold honourably in memory that the holy virgin Mary, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, was made mother of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who is God and man, through whom we supplicate the Father; and we ought to share the faith and believe that, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God was born of her, and her virginity was not violated. *And also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.* *Apostolus* in our language means one sent. *Martyr* we call a witness. They are called apostles because they were sent by Christ. They are called martyrs because they are witnesses that Christ suffered for us, and they themselves [suffered] for Christ.

21. *Therefore, Lord, we pray you, graciously accept this offering of our service, and of your whole household.* The priest commends his own offering and that of all who serve God, that is, who serve the Lord, that it may please the Lord, and that he may be gracious to us. *And order our days in your peace, and command that we be snatched from eternal damnation and numbered in the flock of your elect; through Christ our Lord.* For that which the priest offers, he ought to pray that the priest may be heard, and the days of all be ordered in peace, and that we be snatched from eternal damnation. Concerning which our Lord Jesus Christ will say to the wicked at the end of the world: *Go, you cursed, into eternal fire*, etc. And [that] we may deserve to be numbered by the holy angels in that flock of his elect, to whom he will say: *Come, blessed of my Father* (Matt. 25:34), and the rest.

22. *Which offering we pray you, O God, deign to make in all things blessed, ascribed, ratified, reasonable and acceptable.* The priest supplicates that the almighty Father may deign to receive as blessed the offering which he offers for himself and for the people, and to hold it ascribed, that is, assigned, so that it may please him. *Ratified*, that is, judged, that he may judge it worthy to be offered in his sight. *Reasonable*: may he deign to make it full of just reason, because it is acceptable to him only if we, believing rightly, offer for a just reason; it is just to ask that the almighty Father, by sanctifying, make that offering which we offer reasonably *become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.* The Son is beloved of the Father, as the Father himself testified from heaven, saying: *This is my beloved Son*, etc. (Matt. 3:17). And we ought to love him, because he first loved us and suffered for us.

23. *Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; with eyes raised to heaven, to you, God, his almighty Father, giving thanks to you, he blessed, broke, and gave to his disciples, saying: Take, and eat of this, all of you: for this is my body. In like manner, after supper, he took also this glorious cup into his holy and venerable hands; again giving thanks to you, he blessed, and gave to his disciples, saying: Take, and drink of it, all of you. For this is the cup of my blood, of the new and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins. As often as you do these things, you shall do them in memory of me.*

24. As to what we passed over: *who on the day before he suffered*, that is, on the day before he suffered for us, he willed to hand over to his disciples his body and blood, a mystery, so that they might hand it on to us. Who would ever believe that bread could be changed into flesh, wine into blood, had not the Saviour himself said it, who created bread and wine and made all things from nothing? It is easier to make something from something than to create all things from nothing. The Saviour himself willed to take on a human body and to join man to God, so that there might be one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus; he willed that bread and wine be offered to him through us, and be divinely consecrated by him, and that the faithful people believe the mystery to be true, which he himself also handed on to his disciples, saying: *Take and eat of this, all of you.* And when he raised his eyes to heaven and gave thanks to the Father, he taught us that we ought always to supplicate the Father, that he may deign to accomplish so great a sacrament through our hands.

25. And when he said, *As often as you do these things, you shall do them in memory of me*, he commanded us to be mindful of his passion; and we ought at all times to be mindful of how much he endured for us, when we celebrate this sacrament, and to place our confidence in his mercy, not in our own goodness. *Wherefore we, your servants, O Lord, and also your holy people, are mindful of Christ, your Son, our Lord.* We priests profess that we are mindful, and we bear witness that the people are mindful, of Christ your Son, our Lord. The priests ought to be faithfully mindful because they themselves celebrate the Mass, for it is a foolish petition if the petitioner does not know what he is asking for. The holy people ought to be mindful because Christ suffered not only for the priests but also for the holy people; it is called [holy] because it has been sanctified by receiving the faith and baptism of Christ.

26. Now they indicate of what they ought to be mindful, that is, *of the blessed passion, and also of the resurrection from the dead, and also of the glorious ascension into heaven.* We ought to be mindful of the passion of Christ your Son, because he deigned to suffer for us; of the resurrection from the dead, [because] through his resurrection [souls] were set free. We ought to remember his glorious ascension, because the human body which he had assumed, joined to the divinity, he carried into heaven by his own majesty, without anyone's help. We said 'without anyone's help' so that it may be understood that he did not ascend into heaven carried by men, or by angels, or by any creature, but was raised up by the Father of majesty, of whom he himself said in the Gospel: *I and the Father are one.*

27. *We offer to your glorious Majesty, from your own gifts and bounty, a pure victim, a holy victim, an unblemished victim, the holy bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation.* O Lord, mindful of all your goodnesses mentioned above, we offer to your Majesty a pure victim, that is, from a pure body, because your body, which we believe comes to be from this bread, is pure. *A holy victim*, because you sanctified your body when you assumed man into God, and now sanctify this bread, that it may become your body. *An unblemished victim*, because you suffered for us without the stain of sin.

28. *The holy bread of eternal life*, because you are the living bread which came down from heaven, and you willed that we receive your body in this bread sanctified by you, and willed that we take your blood through the cup of your passion: sanctify this victim, that it may become for us your body and your blood. *Upon which deign to look with a favourable and serene countenance.* This we pray: that the holy Father may deign to look upon the good things offered by us with a kind, gentle and bright countenance, that is, to see them and hold them accepted. *As you deigned to hold accepted the gifts of your servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice, an unblemished victim.* The Lord held Abel's gifts accepted, because he offered to the Lord whatever best he found; and we too ought to offer just and clean gifts to God with a clean heart. Abraham did not spare his own son Isaac, but, obedient to the Lord's command, was willing to offer him.

29. Melchizedek was the first priest to offer bread and wine to the Lord, and therefore it is written in the Psalm: *You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek* (Ps. 109:4). For as Melchizedek [offered] bread and wine, so Christ too in his passion offered his body and blood to God the Father for us, and willed that we imitate the mystery of his passion in bread and wine, when, giving his disciples bread and the cup, he said: *This is my body, and this is the cup of my blood.* And we ought to supplicate that, as the gifts of the aforesaid Fathers were acceptable to God, so ours may be too.

30. *We humbly beseech you, almighty God, command these to be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high, in the sight of your divine Majesty.* We humbly ask that the heavenly Father command our gifts, offered upon this altar which can be seen, to be carried by the hands of his holy angel to that high altar before his divine Majesty, which we cannot see with our eyes, because it is not bodily but spiritual. And just as we cannot search out the divine Majesty of the Father, so neither ought we to search out the things that are in his sight, but rather believe [them]: *that as many of us as, by this partaking of the altar, receive the most sacred body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.* We ought to pray the heavenly Father that all of us who from that altar, upon which we offer to God the Father in commemoration of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, receive the [body] and blood of the aforesaid Son, may deserve to receive every heavenly blessing, through Christ our Lord.

31. *To us sinners also, your servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some part and fellowship with the holy apostles and martyrs and all the saints.* All these sacrifices have been offered, by the priest as well as by the people, so that almighty God may not reckon our sins, but grant us a portion with his saints. *Into whose company, we pray, admit us, not as a weigher of merit but as a bestower of pardon.* This we ask: that he who said, *On whatever day a sinner is converted and does penance, all his sins shall be in oblivion before me*, may not weigh out a requital for sins, but may himself (be) the bestower of pardon, so as to bring us into the fellowship of the saints, through Christ our Lord.

32. *Through whom* he created all these gifts; may he sanctify and bless them, and may they profit us, so that through Christ, through whom all things were made, and in Christ, in whom all things were made, and with whom all things were made, who is coeternal with the Father, we may ever give thanks to the Father for ever and ever. Amen. *Admonished by saving precepts and [formed] by divine [instruction]*, etc. We have been admonished and commanded by the precepts of Christ, which are full of salvation, because he himself is eternal salvation, and formed by divine instruction; that is, we have received the form and example from Christ our Lord, and have dared to pray as he taught his disciples; and we believe [him to be] our Father, who created us, and we say:

33. *Our Father, who are in heaven.* Christ said after his resurrection: *I ascend to my Father and your Father.* He said 'his Father' in one sense and 'our Father' in another. 'His Father', because he is the proper Son of the Father, begotten of the Father's substance before all ages, coeternal with the Father. He is 'our Father' because he created us in time, and we are adoptive sons, and we shall possess the heavenly inheritance of our heavenly Father if we fulfil in works what we promised at the reception of the faith. *Caelum* (heaven) is so called from *celare* (to hide), because it hides the divine secrets. Otherwise *caelum* is named from *celsitudo* (loftiness), because it is higher than earthly things. We say *Our Father, who are in heaven* to show that we believe in the heavenly Father; and as sons long to fulfil the precepts of their father, so may we too desire to fulfil his precepts and always to strive towards heaven.

34. *Hallowed be your name*, that is, that we may be worthy to hold his holy name in our hearts, so that, as the holy angels who are in heaven know and understand the holiness of his name, so we too who are on earth may, with his help, deserve to know his holiness; so that his name may be hallowed on earth as in heaven. *Your kingdom come*, that is, that we may deserve to know his kingdom and power, and that the devil may no longer reign over us because of our sins, but his kingdom may come, as is written in the Gospel: *The kingdom of God is within you.*

35. *Your will be done, on earth as in heaven*: that is, that as those who are in heaven do his will, so we who are on earth may do it. *Terra* (earth) is so called from *terere* (to tread), because it is trodden by feet. *Give us this day our daily bread.* *Pan* among the Greeks is translated 'all' in our language. And we pray that the almighty Father may deign to bestow on us at all times all sustenance, spiritual and bodily. *And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.* For he does nothing unjust who demands a debt from one who owes him; but if almighty God demands all our debts from us, no one without doubt is found free; and therefore we ought to forgive our debtors their debts, so that the Almighty may forgive us ours, because he himself said: *If you do not forgive, each of you, your brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins* (Matt. 18:35). And elsewhere: *All scandals are removed from his kingdom* (Matt. 13:41); and again, a sacrifice is not received if it is offered with a scandal, but it is commanded to be left before the altar until one is reconciled to one's brother, and then to be offered with a clean heart.

36. *And lead us not into temptation.* That is, that we may not enter into that temptation in which the devil tempts us, and consent to him; but that the Lord himself may defend us, so that we are not led into the devil's temptation, because if the Lord lets us go, at once we are led into the devil's snare; and therefore we ask that he himself deliver us *from evil*, that is, from every assault of the devil. *Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils past, present and to come.* We ask this, that he may deliver us from all evils, he who created us clean and good, in whom there is no evil. Past [evils] are those which we have already committed by sinning before, and for which we therefore endure scourges. Future [evils] are those which may yet come at the devil's prompting; and therefore we pray to be delivered from all, because in the sight of God nothing is past or future, but all things are present.

37. *With the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, interceding for us, and the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and Andrew.* We call to our aid the Mother of God, who was a virgin before giving birth, a virgin in giving birth, a virgin after giving birth; and the blessed apostles, who handed down to us the mysteries to be celebrated, that they may intercede for us, because we ourselves are not worthy to merit pardon for past and present [sins], nor protection against future ones, unless it is granted to us through their prayer. We have already prayed to be delivered from evils; now let us pray that, through the intervention of the aforesaid saints, he who is able to deliver from evil may graciously grant peace in our days.

38. Peace from the temptation of the devil, that we may not be led into it; peace from evil men, that we may not suffer their scourges. *That, aided by the help of your mercy*, that is, aided by God's help, *we may be always free from sin and safe from all disturbance*: that is, our sins having been forgiven in the present age, we may not be disturbed by sinning again, nor suffer eternal disturbance on the day of judgement. *The peace of the Lord be always with you.* Christ is the eternal peace, who reconciled us to the Father through his passion, so that we should not be held in hell because of the sin of the first man. The priest prays this, that that peace may remain with the people and make all of one mind, so that we may deserve to reign peaceably with Christ in heaven.

39. And therefore we make peace then, before we receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ into our bodies, because without concord we are not worthy to receive the holy communion. For gifts are not received by the Lord if we are at discord with our neighbours, before we are reconciled. Then the clergy pray, singing: *Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.* He is called Lamb because of innocence, since it harms no one, neither men nor beasts; and when it is led to sacrifice, it does not hurt the one who kills it, but after its killing it nourishes its killer. So too Christ harmed no one, as the Apostle says: *Who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth* (1 Pet. 2:22). But after his passion he nourishes many of his persecutors, once converted, through the holy communion of his body and blood, and makes them believers. He took away the sin of the world when he gave us pardon of sins.

40. For before his passion the just and sinners went down into hell, and in the Old Testament we nowhere read of the remission of sins. But Christ through penance promised us not only the remission of sins but also angelic joy, saying: *There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance* (Luke 15:7). We ask Christ himself, who is the innocent Lamb of God, who suffered for the salvation of the world, to have mercy on us, saying: *Have mercy on us.* For in the Old Testament too a lamb was offered for the sins of the people; and in the New Testament Christ offered himself to God the Father, to free the human race from sin by his passion; and therefore the *Lamb of God* is sung at the time when the body and blood of Christ are received, so that we may all believe that then is taken the body and blood of that very Lamb who by dying took away the sins of the world, and by rising again gave us eternal life, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

41. And when the Mass is finished the deacon says: *Go, it is the dismissal.* *Diaconus* is Greek; in Latin it is called *minister* (servant). He announces to the people that the prayers are finished, because no one ought to leave the church before it has been announced by the minister; and all respond: *Thanks be to God.*
